title: Glass house
context: Something tiny built a see-through home with hundreds of neat little windows.
question: What is it?

img.file: Coscinodiscus oculus-iridis (Ehrenberg) Ehrenberg 1840 diatom shell. Colored SEM image.jpg
img.author: Pavel.Somov
img.alt: A round green disc covered in rows of tiny holes, like a perforated plate.

hints: It lives in water and makes its food from sunlight.
Its shell is made of glass (silica).
why: A coloured electron-microscope image of the shell of a diatom, a single-celled alga far smaller than a grain of sand.
pearl: Diatoms build their shells out of glass. These tiny algae make roughly a fifth of the oxygen produced on Earth.

title: Red alert
context: A shiny red surface dotted with little yellow specks. Found in a punnet near you.
question: What is it?

img.author: rich caulton
img.alt: Glossy red skin dotted with small yellow seed-like specks.

hints: It's a fruit that wears its seeds on the outside.
Often dipped in chocolate or served with cream.
why: A close-up of a strawberry's skin, with the little yellow 'seeds' sitting in dimples.
pearl: The 'seeds' on a strawberry are actually tiny fruits called achenes, each holding a seed. An average strawberry has about 200 of them.

title: I see you
context: A huge dome made of thousands of tiny tiles. It's watching you right now.
question: What is it?

img.author: Solomon Christopher
img.alt: A curved brown dome covered in a fine grid of tiny facets.

hints: It belongs to an insect that hunts on the wing.
Each tiny tile is a separate lens.
why: A close-up of a dragonfly's compound eye. Each tiny facet is a separate lens.
pearl: A dragonfly's compound eyes have up to about 30,000 lenses each, giving it almost all-round vision for catching prey in mid-air.

title: Chilly spikes
context: Feathery white blades grew here overnight without a single drop of rain.
question: What is it?

img.file: Hoar frost ice crystals in Tuntorp 13.jpg
img.author: W.carter
img.alt: Spiky, feathery white ice crystals against a dark background.

hints: You'd find it on a cold, clear morning.
It melts in your hand.
why: Hoar frost: ice crystals that grew on a cold surface overnight.
pearl: Hoar frost forms when water vapour in the air turns straight into ice, skipping the liquid stage. 'Hoar' is an old word for grey-white.

title: Heavy lifter
context: Elbowed feelers, a shiny armoured head and a very busy schedule.
question: What is it?

img.author: United States Geological Survey
img.alt: A grey, finely grooved insect head with a bent antenna and a compound eye.

hints: It lives in a colony with a queen.
It might march in a line across your kitchen bench.
why: An electron-microscope image of an ant's head, showing its bent antennae and grooved armour.
pearl: Ants have no lungs. Air seeps into their bodies through tiny holes along their sides called spiracles.

title: Nosy parker
context: A tiny armoured critter with a very long snout. It may have moved into your flour.
question: What is it?

img.author: Louisa Howard, Dartmouth Electron Microscope Facility
img.alt: A small oval beetle with a long downward-curving snout, in grey electron-microscope detail.

hints: It's a beetle.
Its long snout has jaws at the tip.
why: An electron-microscope image of a snout beetle, better known as a weevil.
pearl: True weevils are one of the biggest animal families on Earth, with more than 80,000 known species.

title: Sticky situation
context: A tangle of feathery hairs with little balls caught all through it.
question: What is it?

img.file: Polen en pelos de abeja SEM.jpg
img.author: Brandon Antonio Segura Torres & Priscilla Vieto Bonilla
img.alt: Feathery branched hairs with small round grains stuck among them.

hints: Those little balls came from flowers.
This hairy insect makes something sweet.
why: An electron-microscope image of a bee's branched hairs, dotted with pollen grains.
pearl: Flying bees build up a small electric charge, so pollen can jump onto their hairs before they even touch the flower.

title: Tiny umbrellas
context: A grey landscape packed with flat, overlapping discs. It's from a plant you might eat.
question: What is it?

img.file: Olive leaf lower surface 469x - SEM MUSE.tif
img.author: Nicola Angeli, MUSE (Museo delle Scienze, Trento)
img.alt: A grey surface covered with flat, round, overlapping scales.

hints: Turn the leaf over: this is its silvery underside.
The tree it grows on gives us a famous oil.
why: An electron-microscope image of the underside of an olive leaf, covered in flat, umbrella-like scales.
pearl: The underside of an olive leaf is covered in tiny umbrella-shaped scales. They give it a silvery shine and help the tree save water in hot, dry summers.

title: Don't step on it
context: Striped spikes radiating out from a dark centre on the sea floor.
question: What is it?

img.author: NOAA/National Marine Sanctuaries
img.alt: Long striped spines fanning out from a dark centre.

hints: It lives in the sea.
Its roe is a delicacy in Japan and around the Mediterranean.
why: A banded sea urchin photographed in Hawaii's Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument.
pearl: A sea urchin's mouth is on its underside and has five teeth. It's nicknamed Aristotle's lantern because the Greek philosopher compared it to a lantern.

title: Tough skin
context: A diamond pattern of spiky little bumps, tropical and sweet underneath.
question: What is it?

img.author: Rhododendrites
img.alt: Green and yellow diamond-shaped segments, each with a small spike.

hints: It's a fruit with a spiky crown on top.
Some people put it on pizza. Others are horrified.
why: A close-up of a pineapple's skin.
pearl: A pineapple isn't one fruit. It's lots of small fruits, one from each flower, fused together. Each diamond on the skin was once a flower.

title: Past its best
context: White and grey fuzz spreading across a dimpled orange surface.
question: What is it?

img.author: gailhampshire
img.alt: Orange dimpled skin with white and grey fuzzy patches.

hints: The dimpled surface is the skin of a citrus fruit.
The fuzz is a fungus.
why: Penicillium mould growing on the skin of an orange.
pearl: This mould is a Penicillium. A cousin, Penicillium roqueforti, gives blue cheese its blue-green veins.

title: Hitchhiker
context: A spiky green ball with tiny hooked tips. It wants to come home with you.
question: What is it?

img.author: Zephyris
img.alt: A round green seed head bristling with long red-tipped hooked spikes.

hints: It's a seed head.
It clings to socks and dog fur.
why: A burr: a seed head covered in tiny hooks.
pearl: Burrs hook onto passing animals so their seeds get carried far away. A plant can't walk, so it hitches a ride.

title: Jumping jack
context: A flat little body built for slipping through fur, with seriously strong back legs.
question: What is it?

img.file: Flea Scanning Electron Micrograph False Color.jpg
img.author: CDC/Janice Haney Carr
img.alt: A pink, flattened insect with long spiny back legs.

hints: Your cat or dog may have met one.
It's a world-class high jumper.
why: A coloured electron-microscope image of a flea.
pearl: A flea can leap around 100 times its own body length, powered by a springy pad of protein called resilin.

title: Big buzz
context: An orange face with huge jaws and two long feelers. It's not here for the honey.
question: What is it?

img.file: Murder hornet 2, face 2020-10-01-18.55.04 ZS PMax UDR (50409447306).jpg
img.author: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
img.alt: An orange insect face with dark eyes, long antennae and big jaws.

hints: It's the world's biggest of its kind.
It's a type of wasp.
why: The face of a northern giant hornet, photographed by the US Geological Survey.
pearl: The northern giant hornet is the world's largest hornet. Queens can grow to about 5 centimetres long.

title: Hairy landscape
context: Bumpy ground covered with odd little knobbly stalks.
question: What is it?

img.author: Louisa Howard, Dartmouth Electron Microscope Facility
img.alt: A bumpy grey surface with scattered knobbly hair-like stalks.

hints: It came from a plant.
It's green in real life and catches sunlight.
why: An electron-microscope image of the top of a flowering tobacco leaf, covered in tiny hairs.
pearl: Many leaves are covered in tiny hairs called trichomes. Some are sticky and trap insects; others release a smell when brushed.

title: Sunny spirals
context: Golden petals around a centre packed with tiny florets in swirling spirals.
question: What is it?

img.file: Close-up sunflower head, New Mexico, U.S.jpg
img.author: NathanScientific
img.alt: A yellow flower head with a centre of tiny florets in spiral rows.

hints: It's a big flower.
Its seeds are a popular snack.
why: The head of a sunflower, with hundreds of tiny florets in the middle.
pearl: A sunflower's seeds sit in two sets of spirals, and the numbers of spirals are usually Fibonacci numbers, such as 34 and 55.

title: Hook, line and...
context: Rows of tiny plastic hooks waiting for something to grab.
question: What is it?

img.author: Olivepixel (Flickr)
img.alt: Rows of small curved plastic hooks.

hints: Its other half is covered in little loops.
It makes a ripping noise when you pull it apart.
why: A close-up of the hook side of a Velcro (hook-and-loop) fastener.
pearl: Swiss engineer George de Mestral invented Velcro after burrs stuck to his dog on a walk. The name blends the French words velours (velvet) and crochet (hook).

title: Achoo
context: A pile of colourful spiky balls and beans. Spring is in the air. Literally.
question: What is it?

img.author: Dartmouth Electron Microscope Facility
img.alt: Many colourful grains: spiky yellow balls, green spheres and beans.

hints: It comes from flowers.
Bees carry it from plant to plant.
why: A coloured electron-microscope image of pollen from sunflower, morning glory, hollyhock, lily, primrose and castor bean.
pearl: Pollen has a super-tough outer coat, so it can survive in mud and rock for millions of years. Scientists use fossil pollen to work out what ancient landscapes looked like.

title: All eyes
context: Two giant red domes nearly meet in the middle of this face.
question: What is it?

img.file: Big eyed fly 2020-08-28-10.45.55 ZS PMax UDR (50287567652).jpg
img.author: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab
img.alt: An insect face with two huge dark red eyes and a yellow middle.

hints: It has just two wings.
It's notoriously hard to swat.
why: A close-up of a fly's face, photographed by the US Geological Survey. Most of its head is eye.
pearl: A fly's compound eyes are made of thousands of tiny lenses. They're brilliant at spotting movement, which is why flies dodge swatters so easily.

title: Garden pest
context: A plump little sap-sucker parked on a leaf, with long thin legs.
question: What is it?

img.author: Arlo James Barnes
img.alt: A grey, pear-shaped insect with thin legs on a leaf surface.

hints: Ladybirds love to eat it.
Gardeners find it clustered on rose stems.
why: An electron-microscope image of an aphid sitting on a plant.
pearl: Some aphids are born already pregnant: a baby aphid can carry its own developing babies inside it.

title: Beach day
context: Shiny black chips, like tiny broken bottles. You might find it between your toes.
question: What is it?

img.author: Renée Janssen
img.alt: Glossy black angular grains under a microscope.

hints: It comes from a beach.
It's made from cooled lava.
why: Grains of black sand from Punaluʻu beach in Hawaii, seen under a microscope.
pearl: Black sand beaches like Punaluʻu form when hot lava hits the sea and shatters into small glassy grains.

title: Don't squash it
context: A shield-shaped head with a long drinking straw tucked underneath.
question: What is it?

img.author: Louisa Howard, Dartmouth Electron Microscope Facility
img.alt: A grey insect head with a long thin beak running down the middle.

hints: It's also called a shield bug.
Squash it and you'll know why it has its name.
why: An electron-microscope image of the head and mouthparts of a stink bug (shield bug).
pearl: Stink bugs release a smelly liquid from glands on their bodies when they feel threatened.

title: Prickly purple
context: A purple tuft on top of a spiky green ball. Handle with care.
question: What is it?

img.author: Tyw7
img.alt: A purple brush-like flower on top of a spiky green bulb.

hints: It's a spiky wildflower.
It's a national emblem in one part of the United Kingdom.
why: A thistle flower: a purple tuft above a spiny green base.
pearl: The thistle is Scotland's national emblem. Legend says a barefoot Norse raider stepped on one and yelled, warning the sleeping Scots.
